title: Final 2026 budget for local boards and shared services
subtitle: Police, library and Wellington social services budgets, housing pressures, provincial downloading, and the mayor's concerns about the tax trajectory.
overview: Council approved the 2026 budget update for local boards and shared services agencies {{vote:m1}}. The package covers Guelph Police Services, the Guelph Public Library, the County of Wellington social services, public health, The Elliott Community, the Grand River Conservation Authority and the Downtown Guelph Business Association. Together with the city's own budget, it sets a net levy requirement of up to $383,403,808. These agencies add 4.40 per cent to the tax levy.

The police, the library and the county's social services each presented. The police and the library lowered their requests after the mayor asked the boards late last year to review their budgets. Wellington County's housing and homelessness spending is the largest source of upward pressure. Delegates said the province and federal government fund too little of it.

Council also agreed to use assessment growth revenue above the budgeted amount to reduce the 2026 levy impact. This departs from the Revenue Budgeting Policy. The mayor said the boards' share of the levy has grown over time and that this trend is unsustainable. The mayor plans to explore further governance or oversight measures ahead of the 2027 budget.

decisions.item: Local boards and shared services operating budget
decisions.detail: Council approved the amended 2026 operating budget for the local boards and shared services agencies, with a net levy increase of $15,458,560, or 4.40 per cent, over 2025.

decisions.item: Police, library and county levy increases
decisions.detail: The budget includes added levy requirements of $6,631,188 for Guelph Police Services, $1,979,286 for the Guelph Public Library and $8,191,200 for the County of Wellington.
Council approved applying assessment growth revenue above the budgeted amount to reduce the 2026 levy impact, contrary to the Revenue Budgeting Policy.
An amended net levy requirement of up to $383,403,808 was approved for the City and its local boards and shared services agencies.
The business association's budget was approved with gross expenditures of $807,754 and a total levy of $742,836.
An amended 2026 capital budget for the local boards was approved at $4,734,300 gross, a net decrease of $514,300 from the adopted budget.

debate: Police staff said the planned catch-up staffing is now being absorbed by unfunded provincial requirements. These are more court security and a return of school-resource officer programs under Bill 33. Staff said the province provides no dedicated funding for these. A police representative also said the service effectively covers about 200,000 people, because of the university population, against roughly 150,000 residents.

Several councillors said provincial downloading is a main driver of rising costs. One councillor said that residents who object to these costs should consider the governments they vote for. Another noted that returning police to high schools reinstates resources that were reallocated when the program ended.

Councillors asked police about measuring the support given to human trafficking victims. Staff said exact victim-support figures were not available and committed to follow up. A councillor also asked for neighbourhood-level police presence. Staff said the downtown gets more presence for now and the goal is to extend it over time.

The library's request rose about 16 per cent, mainly from staffing for the new central library and recent collective agreements. The board deferred some hiring and cut a major IT project. Councillors asked about operating costs and sponsorship. Library staff said they plan a branch network review after the new library opens and that fundraising has exceeded its goal.

County staff said homelessness, rent supplement and winter response costs drive the 18.5 per cent city levy increase for social services, since provincial prevention funding has stayed flat. Staff said the funding mostly holds the line on homelessness. Delegates also described long childcare wait lists and a gap that bars subsidy for families using childcare not enrolled in the $10-a-day program.
